Atmos Rewards offers six communities, each with its own travel perks and opportunities to earn bonus points

Atmos Rewards is the airline loyalty program for Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines. One of its newer features is Atmos Communities, which offer additional rewards and benefits tailored to different travel interests.

There are six communities, including two reserved for Alaska and Hawaii residents. The other four are open to members regardless of where they live. But don’t get caught up in the community names. The best choice for you may depend more on your travel plans than the groupings suggest.

Here’s how to decide which Atmos Community best fits your travel patterns.

Atmos Communities are like groups within the Atmos Rewards program that offer additional benefits based on different travel interests.

They’re free to join for Atmos Rewards members. Four communities are available to all members, while community Club 49 is reserved for Alaska residents and community Huaka’i by Hawaiian is reserved for Hawaii residents.

You can belong to only one community at a time and switch communities once per calendar year. Consider your upcoming travel plans before choosing.

Joining a community is easy: Log in to your Atmos Rewards account and navigate to “Account overview.” Select “Join a Community,” browse the options and click the “Join” button under the one you choose.

Each Atmos Community has a list of 10 destinations where members can earn bonus points and status points. Although the destinations differ by community, the rewards structure is the same.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, members can earn up to 10,000 bonus points and 10,000 status points by visiting qualifying destinations.

Here’s how many points you’ll earn as you reach each milestone:

Visit one destination, earn 100 status and bonus points.

Visit two destinations, earn 200 status and bonus points.

Visit three destinations, earn 300 status and bonus points.

Visit four destinations, earn 400 status and bonus points.

Visit five destinations, earn 500 status and bonus points.

Visit six destinations, earn 750 status and bonus points.

Visit seven destinations, earn 1,000 status and bonus points.

Visit eight destinations, earn 1,250 status and bonus points.

Visit nine destinations, earn 2,500 status and bonus points.

Visit 10 destinations, earn 3,000 status and bonus points.

The first member of each community to visit all 10 qualifying destinations during the challenge period will also earn 100,000 bonus points.

New lists of qualifying destinations for each community take effect on Jan. 1, 2028.

Here’s a closer look at the six communities, their benefits and the destinations eligible for bonus points.

Global Locals is geared toward frequent international travelers. Benefits include:

Earn 10% more status points toward Atmos elite status on flights that begin and/or end outside the U.S., including award flights.

Earn 1 status point for every 25 points transferred to Atmos Rewards from Bilt or Marriott Bonvoy.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these 10 Oneworld Alliance hubs count toward bonus points and status points. Qualifying layovers also count toward the destination challenge, so you don’t necessarily need to make these cities your final stop.

If you frequently travel internationally or have any upcoming flights through any of these airports, including qualifying layovers, Global Locals might be a fit for you.

If you have the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card, you’ll earn 3 Atmos points per $1 spent on eligible Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, dining and foreign transactions. The last bonus category can be especially useful for frequent international travelers.

This community has a similar setup to Global Locals, but most of its bonus destinations are in the U.S. Here’s what you can get:

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus:

This community would be an excellent choice if your upcoming travels include several of these airports, even if dining isn't the main reason for your trips. If dining out is one of your favorite activities, check out the best credit cards for restaurants.

Active Escapes focuses on airports in outdoor-oriented destinations that are all in the U.S., save one. Benefits here are:

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus:

While these airports are gateways to national parks and other natural attractions, you don’t have to be an outdoor enthusiast to benefit. Like before, don’t let the heading sway you. Rather, consider the destinations before you decide.

Families On the Go might appeal to you if you redeem Atmos Rewards for your children. Benefits include:

Get 20% of your points back on eligible award flights for kids 12 and under after you complete your trip.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, these destinations qualify for bonus points and status points:

This community may be especially valuable if you regularly book award flights for children 12 and under. Even if you don't travel with kids, it could be worth considering if its qualifying airports align better with your travel plans than those of other communities.

Exclusively for Alaska residents, Club 49 offers rewards that are focused on travel to, from and within the state:

Two free checked bags when traveling to or from Alaska on Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines.

Three free checked bags when traveling within Alaska on Alaska Airlines.

Two Travel Now discounts per year for 30% off one-way refundable Y-class fares on Alaska Airlines, booked within four days of departure for travel to, from or within Alaska.

Ship cargo within Alaska for $49 plus tax (weight, size and content limits apply).

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Baggage benefits don’t combine with other free checked bag allowances, such as those that come with some Alaska credit cards. However, they apply to everyone traveling on the same reservation.

Through Dec. 31, 2027, here are the 10 destinations that count toward the bonus offers:

While this community is only for Alaskans, you might decide one of the other communities more closely matches your travel plans — especially if you already have an Alaska credit card with free baggage benefits. However, if you ship a lot of cargo or think you’ll use the Travel Now discounts, those are special benefits that may sway you to choose Club 49.

Hawaii residents have their own community just for them: Huaka’i by Hawaiian. It offers benefits focused on interisland travel:

Two free checked bags on neighbor island flights on Hawaiian Airlines, including sports equipment like surfboards and golf bags.

Quarterly fare discounts of 10% off one neighbor island booking, or 20% off for eligible Hawaiian Airlines® World Elite Mastercard® and Atmos™ Rewards Visa® cardholders.

Earn 50% more points and status points on flights between Hawaiian islands beginning Jan. 1, 2027.

Get 20% off Atmos Rewards Unlocked experiences.

Seven destinations are in Hawaii, with one on the mainland and two international cities. If you live in Hawaii and like to hop between islands, this community is a strong choice.

Don’t be persuaded by the names of the communities. Look a little deeper, because there’s a lot of overlap between destination lists. Compare the options against your upcoming travel plans.

You can change communities once per calendar year, so you aren’t locked in to your initial choice indefinitely. However, switching communities resets your destination-challenge progress, but you’ll retain any points you’ve already earned.

If your home airport (or one you visit frequently) is already on a community’s list, you may have an easier time earning points. Also consider whether a particular community benefit, such as free checked bags or points back on award flights for kids, outweighs the destination challenge.

Finally, pay attention to airport codes. For example, Tokyo’s Narita (NRT) and Haneda (HND) appear on different community lists. New York’s qualifying airport is JFK, while it is DCA in Washington, D.C. If you have a choice between airports, check which one qualifies for your community’s challenge.

#2999. Arm vs. Marvell Technology: Which Artificial Intelligence Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Arm's licensing model dominates mobile, while Marvell's networking silicon powers AI data centers, but their valuations and risk profiles diverge sharply.

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 6:50PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Arm Holdings ›

The expansion of artificial intelligence has pushed investors toward high-growth hardware providers. Choosing between Arm Holdings (ARM -14.09%) and Marvell Technology (MRVL -11.69%) requires a careful look at their different roles in the chip ecosystem.

Arm provides the energy-efficient architecture used in almost every smartphone, while Marvell specializes in high-speed networking and data center infrastructure. Both companies are positioned to benefit from the rising demand for accelerated computing, yet they offer distinct risk profiles and valuation levels. This comparison helps you determine which path fits your investment strategy through 2027.

In the rapidly evolving world of semiconductor stocks, Arm is unique because it did not actually manufacture chips historically. Instead, it designs the primary architecture and licenses its intellectual property. Its energy-efficient designs are in over 99% of smartphones, although the company is now expanding into cloud data centers and automotive applications, and plans to produce its own chips at last.

The company has shifted toward more complete chip designs to command higher royalty rates. This model creates a high-margin recurring revenue stream. Since it serves almost every major chipmaker, it sits at the heart of the tech sector.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $5.5 billion, representing growth of 23.8% compared to the prior year. This expansion is supported by the adoption of its latest v9 architecture, which carries higher royalty rates than previous generations. The company reported net income of $936.0 million during this period.

As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.1x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to help you understand how much a company relies on borrowing. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with current assets, was a robust 6.0x.

In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, free cash flow reached $979.0 million. Free cash flow is the cash remaining after a business pays for operations and equipment. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

Marvell focuses on the infrastructure that makes modern data centers and telecommunications networks possible. The company specializes in data processing units, networking silicon, and storage controllers. Its recent growth is driven by the need for high-speed connectivity between servers in artificial intelligence clusters.

The company faces significant customer concentration, as its ten largest customers represented roughly 82% of net revenue in its latest annual report. One distributor accounted for approximately 37% of sales, which adds a layer of risk to the business. Despite this, its specialized silicon is vital for major cloud service providers.

In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached $9.5 billion. This reflects a growth rate of 30.6% over the previous twelve-month period. During this same window, the company generated net income of $2.6 billion, showing significant improvement from previous years.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, indicating a low reliance on debt. The current ratio stood at roughly 2.0x, indicating a healthy ability to meet short-term financial commitments.

In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow.

Arm faces risks related to the concentration of the smartphone market. If global phone sales slow, its royalty revenue could stagnate. The company also competes with open-source alternatives like RISC-V, which some manufacturers may prefer to avoid licensing fees. Furthermore, its heavy reliance on the licensing model means any loss of key partnerships with giants like Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) or Qualcomm (QCOM -7.45%) could impact its long-term growth prospects.

Marvell Technology deals with significant customer concentration and geopolitical uncertainty. Trade restrictions and export controls regarding China have created supply chain challenges and impacted demand. The company is also navigating a massive $115 billion all-stock acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE -13.94%), which carries integration risks and potential shareholder dilution. Additionally, it recently settled patent litigation with Credo Technology Group Holding (CRDO -15.20%), highlighting the constant legal threats in the specialized silicon market.

Marvell Technology appears more attractive on a valuation basis, offering lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio multiples than Arm.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

For investors seeking exposure to the artificial intelligence boom, Arm and Marvell are two compelling stocks to own. Between the two, I would prioritize picking up shares of Marvell going into 2027.

Marvell sports a much lower share price valuation than Arm, providing a greater opportunity for a superior return. Arm arguably deserves the elevated valuation multiples because of its high-margin licensing moat. However, given its foray into making its own semiconductor chips, it risks compressing those robust margins due to manufacturing costs.

Marvell's stock was beaten down after it announced it was acquiring Lumentum. I think the acquisition is a smart move. Lumentum provides high-speed optical capabilities for transferring massive amounts of data, a key competitive advantage to winning AI customers. The appeal of Lumentum's solutions is illustrated by its sales of $1.3 billion for its fiscal first quarter, ended Sept. 26, which represented 137% year-over-year growth.

Moreover, Marvell's business is exploding. It generated revenue of $8.2 billion in its 2026 fiscal year, ended Jan. 31, 2026, and the company expects sales to soar to a range between $70 billion to $90 billion by its 2031 fiscal year. That growth does not include Lumentum's sales. With a lower valuation and spectacular, multi-year growth ahead, Marvell looks like the better stock to buy now.

#2998. Steve Kerr, coaching staff tasked with burden of lifting impaired Warriors

Steve Kerr, coaching staff tasked with burden of lifting impaired Warriors originally appeared on NBC Sports Bay Area

SAN FRANCISCO – After sinking from inspirational to abominable following one cataclysmic instant, the Warriors returned home this week hoping to find their way back to mediocrity.

That, after all, was the reasonable expectation in the absence of Stephen Curry, whose oblique strain sustained 11 days ago left the Warriors, then 8-3, without their physical nerve center and emotional support sniper.

If Curry's teammates could win 50 percent of their games without him, that would defy history; the Warriors have lost 63 percent of their games when he is sidelined. They were 7-2 this season with him before the injury – splitting two games on his mandated rest nights – and they are 0-4 without him.

These were not ordinary losses but public spankings.

Until Curry returns, and there is no timeline, the burden of being competitive will get heavier on the heads of coach Steve Kerr and his staff, along with the primary players on the roster.

Can the Warriors get greater impact from veterans like Draymond Green, De'Anthony Melton and reserves Al Horford and Georges Niang? Can youngsters Yaxel Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski, who rank behind only Curry in offensive production, recover from a forgettable road trip?

"The game is obviously harder for everybody without Steph, but especially the guys who have to take on the ballhandling and scoring role," Kerr said Saturday after practice. "I don't love that conversation, particularly for those two guys. That with Steph out, they have to do this, they have to do that. We have to do this, or we have to do that.

"If our execution isn't good, we can't expect them to make something out of nothing. If we can execute better . . . and that's what today's practice was about, and that's what the last couple of days have been about for our staff. Understanding why we're not executing better and giving our guys something to hang their hats on offensively and that's our job. That's what we've been working on."

Can't it be difficult, particularly for young players with expectations, to avoid the pitfall of believing they must fill some of the void created by a missing superstar?

"It's challenging," Podziemski conceded. "It's human nature. It's ego. It's pride. You want to showcase what you can do. That's for everybody."

Podziemski struggled to find his footing, and Lendeborg spent the entire road trip out of sorts, as if the inner "dawg" that was so visible through the first 11 games had gone astray. Aside from a 20-point second half in a 21-point loss to the sorry New Orleans Pelicans, he rarely was a presence. He clearly was affected by his inability to excel in an elevated role.

"That's why I'm (Yaxel's) coach, and that's why I talked to him today," Kerr said. "He's a rookie and he's three weeks (four weeks) into this thing. He's learning and he's growing. And it's my job to help him."

Lendeborg's intricate path to the NBA required considerable mental fortitude, which suggests he'll probably restart his engine and get back to hooping, maybe as soon as Sunday against the impressive Boston Celtics.

But navigating such circumstances while chasing potential can be tricky.

"When your best player is out, I think there's a natural instinct to look inward and say what do I need to do more of, for everybody one through 15," Podziemski said. "But when you think about it that way, it harms the team more than helps because you're putting yourself before the team. If you just think about what the team needs, no matter if Steph is in or out, whatever you're good at just bring that to the table."

Losing five consecutive games following an eight-game win streak has the entire operation trying to fix what's broken. There's no suitable replacement for what Curry brings, so it's about limiting mistakes – and there have been plenty on offense and defense – and the Warriors reminding opponents they came to play.

Not for a few possessions or even a full quarter. For all 48 minutes.

"There's no magic pill to it," Kerr said. "It's everything. It's a comprehensive game. If our defense improves, our offense will improve. But it has to start on the defensive end. We can't sit here and say we need to replace Steph's scoring, or we need to throw the ball to so-and-so. It's defense, defense, defense. Grit, competitiveness, fighting.

"Our offense will come from that. We will make some tweaks, no question, but it is it's not about the tweaks. It's about the competitive fire."

That's the surest way for the Warriors to be competitive with Curry, and it's the only way they can compete without him. Sure, they opened the season generally projected to hover around .500. Mediocrity until Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody return when the calendar flips to 2027.

Golden State's eight-game win streak raised the bar, as the Warriors looked like a playoff-caliber team. The ensuing five-game losing streak lowered the bar, as they were like one of the worst teams in the league.

As much as Curry means to this team, it has enough to climb out of the mudhole that formed with five consecutive losses an average of 23.2 points. And, yes, the rise must start with defense.

TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased today, but borrowing costs are still expensive for many home buyers.

Mortgage rates dropped today, but anything above 7% still puts pressure on home buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a big reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

If PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.74% or higher.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

#2995. Berkshire Hathaway's Next Big AI Bet Could Be Hiding in Plain Sight

Berkshire Hathaway is a conglomerate with notable exposure to two sectors benefiting from AI's growth.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:15PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%)(BRKB -0.36%) isn't exactly seen as an artificial intelligence (AI) play. But it may have more exposure to this emerging technology than you realize. In fact, the company's large utility and energy operations present opportunities for AI-related investment that are hiding in plain sight. Here's what you need to know and what Berkshire Hathaway could easily do to increase its AI bets.

Berkshire Hathaway is usually classified as a finance business, which isn't a bad place to put it. After all, it has large insurance operations. However, the company is really a massive conglomerate, with businesses including insurance, utilities, energy, manufacturing, housing, and retail, to provide just a short list and high-level view. In Greg Abel's first annual letter as CEO, he reported that the company had 51 non-insurance operating businesses. In a previous letter, former CEO Warren Buffett said the company owned 189 operating businesses. The definition of an operating business is probably responsible for the two different numbers, but either one you pick, the number is huge.

There is a lot hiding inside Berkshire Hathaway. But, notably, it breaks out a few large businesses, including railroads, utilities, and energy. The last two are increasingly tied to the artificial intelligence industry. The company's utility operations provide the electricity that powers AI. The energy business helps supply the natural gas that lets utilities, and increasingly AI companies, generate electricity.

To be fair, Berkshire Hathaway could easily afford to buy a technology business with its cash hoard of more than $370 billion. Only technology isn't really the type of business that Berkshire Hathaway tends to buy. Former CEO Warren Buffett long focused on acquiring boring businesses that were well run and attractively priced at the time of purchase. For example, trains, utilities, and pipelines. Greg Abel's acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison Home for $8.5 billion suggests he's not going to suddenly shift directions.

It would be exciting if Berkshire Hathaway went out and bought a giant U.S. utility, such as NextEra Energy (NEE -0.41%), or a large pipeline business, such as Enterprise Products Partners (EPD -0.91%). While Greg Abel probably wouldn't target companies of that scale, the CEO could certainly afford to buy smaller players in either sector.

But that's not necessary. Both the utility and midstream sectors are capital intensive. Utilities own massive power plants that take years to build and require huge sums of money. Midstream companies are no different, with their pipelines, storage, refineries, and transportation assets. It isn't unusual for a utility or midstream company to have multi-billion-dollar capital investment plans extending as far as five years into the future.

What that means is Berkshire Hathaway could make very large capital investments within its existing operations. And that, in fact, is probably the most likely outcome. The cash on the company's balance sheet, meanwhile, means it could easily afford the required spending. Speaking to the utility and energy segment, Greg Abel noted at the start of 2026 that, "Infrastructure built for hyperscalers and data centers must be paid for by those customers and reflect the risks tied to step-changes in long-term demand." Increasingly, data center operators appear willing to do just that.

For example, Chevron (CVX +0.91%), a longtime holding in Berkshire Hathaway's stock portfolio, has agreed to build a power plant that will use Chevron-produced natural gas to supply dedicated power to data centers. Berkshire Hathaway could do something similar with relative ease.

Berkshire Hathaway is unlikely to start buying up AI technology businesses. That's just not what the company does. However, if you dig into the conglomerate's operations, you see that it still has material opportunity to invest in the AI sector. And while it would be exciting if Greg Abel augmented the company's utility and energy operations through new acquisitions, it is far more likely that Berkshire Hathaway will simply invest in its own operations to benefit from AI growth over time. That's the opportunity that is hiding in plain sight.

#2992. Stifel Says SpaceX Could Buy Stalled Data Centers for One Reason: Their Power. Here’s Why Electricity Is the Real Asset.

There is increasing pushback against AI because of its impact on the power grid, but that's also an opportunity.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:01PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Bloom Energy ›

Wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor. But they do have an advantage since they are often industry experts. This is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann's suggestion that Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) could buy up stalled data centers is so interesting.

The key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power. Here's why this is so important and what it could mean for your stock selection process as you look at companies like Bloom Energy (BE -15.30%), NextEra Energy (NEE -0.41%), and Brookfield Renewable (BEP -2.97%).

SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers.

As the backlash against AI data centers grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly important and contentious issue. Which is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann thinks SpaceX could end up buying data centers that have dedicated power agreements in place. However, you don't need to play this specific angle to benefit. Increasingly, AI companies are being forced to supply their own power. And there are a handful of companies that look set to benefit, including Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable.

Bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. Notably, each fuel cell it sells comes along with a long-term service contract, creating an annuity-like income stream. The company's products are factory-built and can be easily deployed wherever they are needed, providing off-grid power. The company has been losing money for years but is likely to be profitable in 2026. That could be an important inflection point for the business.

But investors are well aware of the opportunity, pushing the stock higher by more than 1,200% over the past three years. With a lofty price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 100x, it is very clearly a well-loved stock. And yet, the opportunity to power AI data centers remains substantial, and perhaps only getting larger. If you are an aggressive growth investor, you should at least consider Bloom Energy, even if you only end up adding it to your wish list.

NextEra Energy is one of the world's largest utilities. In fact, it is looking to get even bigger, with its proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy (D -0.56%). Notably, Dominion's regulated electricity operations include one of the world's most important data center markets. The pairing will also vault NextEra into the number two spot with regard to U.S. nuclear power generation. Basically, NextEra looks like it is doubling down on electricity demand and AI at the same time.

But there's an interesting twist here. NextEra is well positioned to benefit from data centers that get attached to the grid. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. You'll also get to collect NextEra's well-above-market 2.9% dividend yield.

For investors looking to maximize the income they generate, Brookfield Renewable and its 5.2% may be even more attractive. The partnership is focused on clean energy, but has a surprisingly diversified portfolio. For starters, it operates hydroelectric, solar, and wind power facilities. It has increasingly been investing in battery storage. And it owns half of Westinghouse, which is one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. On top of that, it is also geographically diversified, with assets located in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. It is a one-stop shop for investors seeking a focused clean-energy investment and for customers seeking renewable energy.

The key here, however, is that Brookfield Renewable largely sells power under long-term contracts outside of the regulated framework. It already has large deals with AI giants Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) and Google. Add in the goal of at least 5% annual distribution growth, and income lovers would be remiss if they didn't at least examine Brookfield Renewable and the AI opportunity ahead of it.

If you think Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann is on to something, you could simply buy SpaceX. That's fine, but it isn't the only takeaway from his insight. The real story is that access to electricity is increasingly important. And you can also play that investment theme with companies like Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable.

#2988. Wolves 104, Grizzlies 95: Defense Downs the Bear

Basketball is a funny thing. One night, the world is obsessed with your offense-capping defensive stalwart and the next you're holding the number one offense in all of basketball to 95 points while that aforementioned rim protector has an incredible game (and still missed some layups).

In a game in which they looked dominant throughout, the Minnesota Timberwolves taught the Memphis Grizzlies that there is joy in being a young, upstart team, but it is still incredibly hard to face off with a capable team on a random Saturday with some of your best players absent.

No, luckily, the Wolves have seemingly learned this lesson.

Minnesota's nine-point margin is significantly smaller than it likely should be after the Grizzlies outscored them by 12 in the fourth quarter. Don't be fooled, this was functionally a wire to wire victory.

The Wolves employed a bit of a platoon plan on offense tonight, spreading usage to each of the starters and allowing Jonathan Kuminga, Jaden McDaniels, and Ayo Dosunmu to all turn in impressive point totals. This Wolves team just keeps showing up and playing well in a way that could not be further from what Wolves fans are used to. Memphis leaned on Cedric Coward and Most Improved Player frontrunner Ty Jerome, but struggled to do much of anything until a garbage time run.

This was a game that put the floor of the Wolves on display more than its ceiling. This was a close win against an admittedly great team with clear weaknesses. If we're going to start there, with the two-in-one ceiling capper and floor raiser, there's only one man to talk about.

Look, the discourse surrounding Rudy Gobert does make sense. He may be the single greatest floor-raising defensive presence since Tim Duncan or Hakeem Olajuwon, but he also makes those two look like Moses combined with prime Escalade on offense.

(And yes, folks, going from being a bad catcher of the basketball to a stone-handed anomaly who is putting up 40ish% on layups is, in fact, a major regression).

Tonight was one of those nights where everything looked decent for Gobert, even if he only scored seven points. Considering the state of the timeline over the past few days – if you are lobbying for Myles Turner, you live in a 2K fanfiction – it was nice to have a reminder of what a *good* Gobert game can look like.

Anytime Minnesota has a great defensive game, everyone will place the flowers at Gobert's feet. This is, after all, exactly what he was supposed to do here. However, the hand-wave of "Gobert was great" doesn't give him his full deserved credit. Memphis did not look at the rim all game. That meant that by the time they got hot, they were in two deep of a hole to get out of.

The man may be an absolute deadbeat, have the health/food knowledge of a yule log (maybe one that's worm-eaten too), but he is an absurdly game-altering talent.

It may be impossible to replace him, and no one seems willing to give up anything of value for him. At that point, it seems the future holds a lot of floor-raising. After tonight, that sounds pretty perfect.

Five different players hit double digits for Minnesota tonight. Jaden McDaniels (25 points on 11/17 from the field), Ayo Dosunmu (19 points), Jonathan Kuminga (16 points on 6/9 shooting), LaMelo Ball (on 50% from the field after a bad stretch), and TJ Shannon Jr. each scored over 10 points, and together they provided all but 17 points in this game.

The headliner is a hyper-efficient Jaden McDaniels game, but it feels like he is destined to never truly empty the clip, instead opting to be a capable third option no matter who he is sharing the court with. Some days, he's the number three guy to Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball; other days, he's letting Greg Monroe initiate the offense while on a 10-day. Tonight, however, he deferred to Kuminga and Ayo as the two turned defense into offense.

However, the real storyline is TJ Shannon, who continues to rise up the depth chart (much to my personal surprise) as another change-of-pace option in attacking the rim. His 15 points in 26 minutes comes after he looked to have found some confidence and comfort in his last few games.

There was a tweet from a few weeks ago that sticks with me about this team. It said the Wolves have on of the best 1-9s in the league, but have the most garbage 10- 15s as well.

Depth is so hard to really pull off, but the Wolves have the right kind of options. Instead of playing around waiting for a loophole, Minnesota just straight up outperformed and out delivered what the Grizzlies could do off the bench.

The Wolves will face off against Julius Randle and the Brooklyn Nets Monday evening, 6:30pm CT on Peacock, as the two former allies will fight over who deserves their low ppg elbow touches. Considering all of this is about raising the floor, the 3-12 Nets probably wish they pursued Gobert instead of Randle.

#2986. Nokia vs. AT&T: Which Telecom Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 8:03PM EST

Connectivity serves as the backbone of the modern economy, but choosing between infrastructure and services requires careful analysis. Investing in Nokia Oyj (NOK -8.27%) or AT&T (T +2.10%) involves balancing network equipment growth against steady subscription revenue.

Nokia focuses on the hardware and software that make networks run, while AT&T is a retail giant providing wireless and fiber service to millions. This comparison examines their business models, balance sheets, and valuations to determine which stock is better for your portfolio.

Nokia is a global connectivity infrastructure company that builds networks across fixed, mobile, IP, optical, and data center systems. The company serves communications service providers, governments, and large enterprises while operating in approximately 130 countries with roughly 78,000 employees. No single customer accounts for more than 10% of revenue, which helps diversify its revenue streams across various regions and sectors.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $22.6 billion, representing revenue growth of 4.1%. The company reported net income of $858.1 million during this period. This growth reflects ongoing investments in network technology as service providers around the world continue to upgrade their existing infrastructure.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.2x, indicating a low level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio of 1.6x shows the company has more than enough assets to cover its short-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $1.6 billion, which is the cash remaining after operating costs and equipment spending.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $128.9 billion, supported by revenue growth of 3.5%. The company generated net income of $13.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of 10.2%. This net margin represents the percentage of revenue that remains as profit after all expenses are paid.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.6x, measuring its total debt against shareholder equity. The current ratio was 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached $19.4 billion, providing significant capital for dividends and network upgrades.

Nokia must contend with intense competition from other global equipment providers in an industry with high research and development requirements. Rapid technological shifts in the 5G and upcoming 6G markets mean the company must constantly innovate to maintain its market share. Geopolitical tensions also carry risks of influencing where the company can deploy its critical national infrastructure projects.

AT&T faces significant risks from increasing competition in the wireless and broadband sectors, particularly from cable providers and businesses like EchoStar (ECHO -8.72%). The company is vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures on network equipment costs. It also faces potential legal liabilities from lead-clad cables and risks associated with labor union contract negotiations for 43% of its workforce.

AT&T appears more attractively valued based on its lower earnings multiple, while Nokia offers a significantly more conservative balance sheet profile.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Weighing whether to invest in Nokia or AT&T comes down to a trade-off between the former's shift toward artificial intelligence infrastructure and balance sheet cleanliness versus the latter's predictable cash flow and higher dividend income. AT&T is the better fit for conservative investors prioritizing passive income and a more attractive valuation.

However, I would buy Nokia for 2027. While AT&T sports a robust dividend yield of about 5%, it has not raised its dividend payment since cutting the amount in 2022. It also holds a lot of debt, as evidenced by its debt-to-equity ratio of 1.6x.

Nokia has the stronger balance sheet, and its focus on AI infrastructure is paying off. In the third quarter, AI and cloud sales soared 123% and customer orders rose 118% year over year.

Nokia's AI radio access network (AI-RAN) technology uses artificial intelligence to intelligently manage traffic on 5G networks for better speed, coverage, and capacity. AI-RAN is still being tested but is approaching commercial deployment. Thanks to its artificial intelligence business, Nokia stock has a higher potential for share price appreciation than AT&T.

#2984. College Scholarship Breakdown: Types, Sponsors and Eligibility at a Glance

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Scholarships vary in what they pay for and who can apply. Understanding the differences can save you time during your application process.

Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

Before you go searching for a scholarship, it's important to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

Scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

These scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s important to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

Merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:

Merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

Merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

Some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that shows more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

Unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

Some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

Athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

Some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

Scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

Veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

The best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:

Think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

Apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a big impact when you add several of them together.

Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

Not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.

#2980. With the Nasdaq in a Correction, Vanguard's Tech ETF Is the Fund I'd Buy Now

The fund's price has slid back to its late-April level. Its earnings didn't slide with it.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:23PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Information Technology ETF ›

The tech sell-off that started in October has become a correction. As I write, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) has dropped around 13% from its all-time closing high, hit on Oct. 6.

The Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT -7.00%) has dropped even more. It finished at $104.99 on Nov. 19, its lowest close since May 4 and around 19% below its own Oct. 6 record of $129.80.

That said, the fund's still up around 12% in 2026 as of this writing, counting dividends.

When the fund was about 10% below its peak in late October, I didn't think it was a bargain yet. At today's price, I do.

The businesses in it have kept growing their earnings as the share price dropped, and I'd be glad to pay the resulting valuation for a fund I plan to hold for years to come.

The fund owns 315 stocks, but a handful of them drive it. As of Oct. 31, Apple was around 18% of its assets, Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) about 17%, and Microsoft about 12%.

These three haven't moved in step. Apple stock is within about 2% of its record as of this writing. Nvidia, though, has fallen about 29% since Oct. 30 alone. By my math, Nvidia by itself is behind about half of the fund's 10% fall since then.

The slide came with a leadership change. Nvidia said on Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. On Nov. 19, California's attorney general followed with an investigative subpoena over whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information might have gone to China, and if the company misled investors about that risk.

But Nvidia's business is still booming. In the third quarter of its fiscal 2027 (the period ending Oct. 25), the company's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion. Data center revenue climbed 110%, and non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share surged 111%. Management also forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion.

In other words, much of the fund's fall has come from investors paying less for the same chip profits, not from those profits dropping.

Vanguard lists the average price-to-earnings ratio of the stocks in the fund, and that number has dropped a lot in the last year and a half. The fund's holdings traded at about 39 times earnings at the end of June 2025 and about 35 times earnings on April 30, 2026. By Sept. 30, the number was about 33 times earnings, and on Oct. 31, it was 29.5 times earnings.

Granted, that last reading came before the latest 10% slide. With earnings held flat, today's price would put the ratio closer to 26 or 27 times earnings.

That's a big shift for a share price that is now right back where it was in late April, when it closed around $103. By my rough math, every share of the fund now carries about a third more earnings than it did then.

The gap to the broader market has shrunk, too. On Oct. 31, the stocks in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF traded at around 24 times earnings, so the tech fund's premium had fallen to about a quarter. For businesses whose profits are still growing this fast, I think the price is fair.

Sure, the fund might keep sliding. A correction can become a bear market (a drop of 20% or more), and the fund is already near that mark. And with three stocks making up almost half of its assets, a tough patch for just one of them can drag on the whole fund.

But a long holding period changes how much a fall like this matters. After all, this year has already shown how quickly the mood can turn.

The fund closed at around $84 on March 30 (adjusted for its 8-for-1 stock split in April), and it then rose about 55% to its Oct. 6 high in just over six months.

No one knows where this sell-off stops. But an investor planning to hold for five or 10 years is largely buying the earnings these companies produce in that stretch. And those earnings seem to have kept climbing through both of this year's sell-offs.

Is the fund worth buying at around $105 a share? I think so. Its valuation has fallen far more than its price, and its largest companies are still growing. I'd buy the fund now, maybe in a few chunks over the coming months, because the sell-off might go further first.

#2978. Mikal Bridges is finding his groove at the right time

Remember when we all said we wouldn't care about the regular season that much after the championship? That lasted long…

As the Knicks stumbled out to a 0-3 start that didn't seem to stabilize that much until this four-game winning streak that's brought them to 10-6 ahead of tonight's game against Indiana, fans didn't seem to have the patience they promised after this same group showed they can be trusted to step up when it counts.

At the center of that impatience was Mikal Bridges, who, despite putting up a second straight awesome playoff run and fully validating the trade by helping hoist a Larry O'Brien Trophy, was the common target early on as he struggled to find his groove.

Through 11 games, he was averaging just 5.9 points a game on a rough 32.9% from the field and 26.5% from deep. He'd be benched early in games where he didn't have it for Landry Shamet, he looked even more apprehensive than usual, and his defense wasn't as impactful as usual.

We've seen bad stretches from Bridges plenty over the last two years, but this was just maddening. The ring was supposed to free him; it was supposed to allow him to tap into the best of his game for extended stretches. The weight was off his shoulders.

Instead, it just seemed to get heavier? At times, it looked like the yips, basketball edition.

But this is why you exercise patience. These guys are champions; they know how to manage the highs and lows. When they look lost, they'll figure it out.

Body language is a big deal sometimes. You started to see him break out of his shell against the Pacers, where he looked for his shot early and often. When his jumper failed him, he got to the rim. He wasn't getting to the line, but he was attacking gaps and making good reads. The activity was back defensively.

He didn't seem to carry this over into Toronto a few days later, but a pep talk from Jose Alvarado might've done the trick:

Suddenly, he was everywhere defensively. A switch seemed to flip, and it looked like he was back in that Boston series. Needing a big late comeback, he set the tone defensively. Everything he did was purposeful, as he was a +15 in the overtime victory.

The offense came back around two nights later when the Knicks really needed it. Despite being -14 in 30 minutes, he put up an efficient 17 points.

The confidence to take shots like these just wasn't there a few weeks ago. He'd miss one or two threes and just stop shooting. He'd subconsciously pass up shots that had been a part of his game for years. It's pivotal that even when the ball isn't going down that a shooter keeps shooting, and we just didn't see that.

This article comes at a great time after he called game against the Blazers on Saturday night, but I think it shows that he's got his confidence back more than anything. Watch back the tape and see if you notice anything:

First, it's the fact that he consciously looks for the ball off the inbound. A big problem with the Knicks' final-possession offense is that they have one look and no backup plan. We saw that against Indiana with KAT and we see it all the time where they just screen for Jalen Brunson to get the ball and get out of the way.

Here, Bridges goes from a screener to releasing to pop up as a backup option. Then, look at this screenshot:

There are three whole seconds left, and Toumani Camara is on a hard closeout. There is nobody near Andre Drummond underneath the basket. If Bridges immediately hits him, it's an easy dunk (or is it, with how bad his finishing has been…)

In some ways, that's the correct read. A broken inbound has left the opponent scrambling and you have an easy, game-tying bucket under the basket. Maybe if he didn't make the shot, this would be discussed more.

Regardless, the confidence of Bridges matters a whole helluva lot more than winning a regular season game. This is a guy you need in April, May, and June, not November. A 26-point blown lead sucks, blowing the first 15+-point second half lead in the regular season since April 2023 sucks, but you want him taking this shot.

Maybe he just doesn't like the Blazers. That's two game-winners against them in his three years as a Knick.

Now, if only Josh Hart can figure it out too…

#2973. Former All-Star has created NBA’s biggest ‘f–king mess’ — and it just keeps getting worse

Situations don't get much uglier than Dejounte Murray's in New Orleans.

The Pelicans guard wants a trade from the franchise, and his relationship with the organization appears beyond repair.

But worst of all, opposing teams reportedly aren't biting, asking for draft compensation just to take him off New Orleans' hands in a trade.

"What a f–king mess," one NBA executive told Yahoo Sports' Kelly Iko this week. "No one wants to touch him."

Dejounte Murray #5 of the New Orleans Pelicans reacts to a call during a game against the Denver Nuggets in New Orleans, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Getty Images

Now, just over two years later, the Pelicans could be forced to give up even more assets to get rid of him.

Two opposing team officials told Sports Illustrated's Chris Mannix they would demand a first-round pick to take on Murray's contract, which pays him $32.8 million this season and includes a $30.8 million player option for 2027-28.

Murray, 30, has appeared in just 54 games since arriving in New Orleans, having suffered a broken hand and a torn Achilles.

Dejounte Murray of the New Orleans Pelicans reacts during a game against the Golden State Warriors in San Francisco, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026. Getty Images

He's averaging 13.4 points and 4.4 assists through nine games this season, shooting just 29.6 percent from beyond the arc.

But his struggles on the court are only part of the problem.

Murray took to social media to lash out at critics earlier this month, suggesting someone within the organization was responsible for negative posts about him.

Dejounte Murray of the New Orleans Pelicans handles the ball against the LA Clippers on Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026, at Intuit Dome in Inglewood, Calif. NBAE via Getty Images

"The sabotage is real!" he wrote in a since-deleted post.

In another since-deleted tirade, Murray went after a Pelicans fan account that highlighted his mistakes during a blowout loss to the Nets.

"You have no f–king clue what we dealing with," Murray, who hasn't played since Nov. 11, wrote on the platform.

ESPN's Brian Windhorst subsequently claimed the Pelicans had sent Murray home following his trade request, while suggesting the guard had become difficult to keep around the team.

"They sent him home," Windhorst said on "The Hoop Collective" podcast.

"NEVER WAS SENT HOME," he wrote in the comments of a Bleacher Report Instagram post.

Murray has reportedly expressed interest in joining the Suns, with Phoenix guard Jalen Green floated as a potential trade piece.

But according to The Athletic's Sam Amick on Friday, recent discussions between the two teams lasted approximately five minutes and gained "zero traction."

The Suns reportedly don't want to take on Murray's contract without getting back draft compensation.

Iko added that Murray's unhappiness dates back to last season and was exacerbated by the Pelicans' drafting of young point guard Jeremiah Fears in 2025.

While the organization is seemingly ready to move forward without him, Murray could find himself stuck in New Orleans for the foreseeable future.

#2971. Forget Flying Roadsters. Tesla Investors Have 3 Bigger Challenges to Watch.

Tesla has never had trouble building hype or excitement for its business, but investors should keep an eye on these challenges.

By Daniel Miller – Nov 22, 2026 at 9:00PM EST

Tesla (TSLA -7.64%) knows how to get people talking and investors hyped. Futuristic vehicles, robotaxis, and humanoid robots give investors plenty to chew on. Those ideas are awesome, but the investment story also depends on less glamorous questions.

Can Tesla defend its customer base? How expensive could its legal battles become? And will its next big manufacturing bet be as lucrative as investors hope?

None of those questions gets answered by an impressive product demonstration (the Roadster). Here are three challenges worth keeping on investors' radar.

Tesla's domestic sales in China dropped 66.1% year over year to 8,817 vehicles in October. China's battery-electric passenger-car market declined just 5.3%, making it difficult to blame Tesla's entire slide on a struggling market.

Tesla's Shanghai factory exports provided a cushion, increasing roughly 66% to 59,012 vehicles. Tesla typically emphasizes exports early in a quarter, so October alone should be taken with a grain of salt. Still, its Chinese retail sales have declined year over year for five consecutive months.

The catch is that competitors are chasing overseas buyers, too, because China's domestic market can't seem to escape a nasty price war. BYD's (BYDDY -4.27%) overseas shipments jumped roughly 103% in October, helping counter sluggish demand and intense price competition at home.

Exports give Tesla another outlet, but they don't give it an escape hatch from competition. The investor question is whether it can defend sales and pricing as rivals expand internationally, because Chinese autos are spreading globally, and rapidly.

Tesla's technology promises also carry a growing legal exposure. An April Electrek analysis estimated potential financial exposure across lawsuits and regulatory matters at $2.7 billion to $14.5 billion. To be clear, that's an outside estimate of possible outcomes -- not an amount Tesla owes, has reserved, or expects to pay.

For something more concrete, consider the Benavides Autopilot case. A jury awarded $129 million in compensatory damages, assigning Tesla 33% of the fault, plus $200 million in punitive damages. Tesla's portion works out to approximately $243 million. The company is appealing, according to its latest quarterly filing.

The legal picture isn't moving entirely against Tesla, either. Its filing also disclosed that an appeals court vacated class certification in a separate driver-assistance advertising case in October. That case returned to the lower court for further proceedings.

Tesla says it cannot reasonably estimate potential losses in these matters. Investors shouldn't treat the $14.5 billion estimate as an incoming invoice, but unfavorable outcomes could still produce substantial expenses or cash payments.

If there's one word Wall Street strongly dislikes, it's uncertainty. Legal uncertainty and potential costs deserve a place alongside the excitement about what Tesla's new businesses bring to the table.

Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around mid-2027 to make room for more Cybercabs. Tesla is choosing where to put valuable manufacturing resources.

Changing direction can be sensible, especially considering the Cybertruck failed to gain traction with consumers. Sticking with a product just because management once loved it would hardly be a winning strategy.

On the flip side, building more Cybercabs isn't the same as building a profitable robotaxi business. Tesla needs enough paying rides to cover vehicles, charging, maintenance, insurance, and fleet operations.

Further, Tesla needs to walk before it can run. There's also a compliance question. In September, federal regulators opened an investigation into Tesla's self-certification that Cybercab meets federal safety standards. To be clear, that inquiry isn't a finding of anything wrong, but it highlights another factor to consider beyond factory production.

Factory floor space doesn't pay shareholders back on enthusiasm or hype alone. Investors need evidence that the business replacing the Cybertruck can generate attractive returns, and right now we have a lot of hype but also many questions.

Tesla's ambitions remain compelling, and also a little daunting, if investors are honest about the company turning from a vehicle manufacturer to more of a technology conglomerate. But defending its customer base at home and abroad, managing legal exposure and regulatory hurdles, and turning robotaxis into a worthwhile business will help determine how much of that promise reaches shareholders.

Enjoy the futuristic vehicles, barrel rolls, and all. Just keep an eye on the business paying to develop that wild future.

Of more interest to local fans is how Utah's young core will bounce back after a horrendous shooting night against the Suns. Jaxson Hayes, who was almost perfect from the floor Friday night, is expected to play after taking a nasty fall in the fourth quarter against the Suns.

#2955. Worried About Nvidia? Buy This Fantastic Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Instead

This company is driving AI, but it's a lot more.

By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ›

Despite outstanding results for its latest quarter, Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) stock keeps sinking. It's down 19% year-to-date, and it's clear that, for the time being, investors are concerned about what's coming up for the artificial intelligence (AI) powerhouse.

Investors like to avoid uncertainty, although no one ever knows what will happen next; the entire episode was unexpected. However, some companies have tried-and-true businesses that can withstand rigorous investor scrutiny, minimizing their risk.

If you're looking for a top AI company that fits the bill, consider Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -9.48%).

Investors are worried about Nvidia for several reasons right now. No one knows what Nvidia will look like without Jensen Huang at its helm, and CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress has said that deals that resemble "circular financing" will be toned down.

The changes in business approach could impact the company's financials, although Kress assured investors that demand is high, and she raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook from 70% to 75%. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing." She said on Nvidia's 2027 third-quarter (ended Oct. 25) earnings call, "Our customers and our partners are with us... We've got this."

Many AI companies are feeling market concern, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). Nvidia is its largest client, overtaking Apple (AAPL -1.90%) in importance, and one of the main beneficiaries of TSMC's expansion to Arizona, its first U.S.-based facility. Kress noted that Nvidia's suppliers and partners are all behind it, and that it has secured the necessary memory and packaging to resume business as normal. She called out Taiwan Semi specifically, saying, "I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us."

TSMC stock is still up 19% year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%), even though it's 25% off its high.

While Nvidia and TSMC's success are to some degree tied together, TSMC had an excellent business before Nvidia, and it can maintain a strong business even if Nvidia does slow down. While Nvidia accounts for 22% of TSMC's revenue, it's been demanding capacity that could go to other players. In the third quarter, high-performance computing, which is where AI is, accounted for 68% of total revenue, up 22% from last year.

The company's broad diversification is one of the features I always point out, and here is a live example of why that's critical. TSMC is a foundry that works with many partner clients globally. It makes semiconductors for all kinds of industries, which is why it can continue to grow even as tech trends and leaders change. There's no reason to panic about Nvidia's dominant position at this time, but whoever is in the lead will likely work with TSMC.

The company's new Arizona location provides greater capacity and helps it avoid tariffs. It also keeps it closer to its U.S. clients. It still has major expansion plans, including more buildings at the Arizona facility, and it has a location in Washington.

Nvidia chips drive AI development, since the hyperscalers use its best-in-class chips. The new Vera Rubin system, which includes chips and computers, is in high demand. But TSMC plays an important role in making that happen, since it has the capacity to keep the chips coming. CEO C.C. Wei noted that there are several approaches to AI development right now, but since TSMC has "technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust," all the players partner with it.

Performance has been fantastic, fueled by AI. Sales increased 41% year over year (currency-neutral) in the third quarter, and gross margin improved by 6.9 percentage points. It was lower sequentially due to higher costs and growth investments. Management repeated that "a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years."

If AI does slow down, Taiwan Semi might, too. It's not a sure thing, but even if it does happen, it isn't likely to last.

At the current price, TSMC stock trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23, which is a fantastic deal on a growth stock that will continue to drive AI development and other technology.

#2951. 49ers’ Colton McKivitz carted off after gruesome leg injury on 'Sunday Night Football'

The San Francisco 49ers lost their starting right tackle Colton McKivitz to a gruesome injury during their Week 11 "Sunday Night Football" game against the Minnesota Vikings.

McKivitz was injured after blocking on a Christian McCaffrey run in the latter half of the second quarter. The 30-year-old tackle was rolled up in a pile as McCaffrey was tackled and as McKivitz came out of the pile, his left foot was facing the wrong direction.

McKivitz's 49ers teammates were immediately upset looking at the tackle's injury. Christian McCaffrey fell to a knee looking at him while Trent Williams was shown on the broadcast looking dismayed, and he forcibly spiked his helmet into the ground.

McKivitz was quickly tended to by medical staff on the field and was carted into the locker room as a result of his injury. Swing tackle Vederian Lowe checked into the game to replace him.

49ers coach Kyle Shanahan provided an update about McKivitz's status after the game. He told reporters McKivitz suffered a fractured and dislocated left ankle and will miss the remainder of the season because of it, per ESPN's Nick Wagoner.

McKivitz entered play Sunday having played all 563 snaps for the 49ers offense, one of two San Francisco linemen to do that along with left guard Connor Colby.

McKivitz was injured while blocking on a Christian McCaffrey run. McCaffrey was tackled on the play and the veteran running back landed directly on the back of McKivitz's left leg.

McKivitz remained down on the field after the play and eventually rolled out of the pile, revealing that his left foot was facing the wrong way.

Vederian Lowe is McKivitz's backup. The five-year veteran was originally selected by the Vikings in the fifth round of the 2022 NFL Draft and has appeared in 55 career games with 25 starts, all of which came with the New England Patriots.

Lowe spent the previous three seasons with the Patriots and was a part of the team that made it to Super Bowl 60. Now, he will be tasked with starting in place of McKivitz with the 30-year-old right tackle set to miss the rest of the season.

The 49ers have four offensive tackles on their 53-man roster. Below is a look at the pecking order within the unit.

Cruz, a fifth-round rookie out of Kansas, is inactive for Sunday's game but will likely be active in future games as the team's swing tackle with McKivitz sidelined.

The 49ers also have Foster Sarell, who has appeared in 41 games (four starts) with the Los Angeles Chargers, and Isaac Alarcon of the International Player Pathway available on their practice squad to help man the position.

Additionally, San Francisco has Austen Pleasants, who appeared in 15 games for them last season with one start, on IR with a return designation. It isn't clear when he will be ready to return, but he could also be an option to replenish the team's tackle depth.

This story will be updated as more information becomes available.
