#2950. Comcast vs. Walt Disney: Which Media Stock Is a Better Buy?

Comcast's cash machine and Disney's prized franchises pull in opposite directions, and the valuation gap between them is hard to ignore.

By Jack Delaney – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 10:00PM EST

Is the future of media found in the cables under the street or the stories on the screen? Investors often choose between Comcast (CMCSA +0.16%) and Walt Disney (DIS -1.89%) for diversified exposure.

Comcast operates as a backbone of modern connectivity while diversifying into world-class entertainment and theme parks. Disney remains the gold standard for intellectual property, using its content library to fuel a massive ecosystem of streaming and travel. Comparing them helps clarify whether you prefer reliable utility-like cash flow or brand-driven growth.

Comcast provides broadband, wireless, and video services to millions of customers, largely under its Xfinity and Comcast Business brands. As one of the prominent media stocks, it also owns NBCUniversal, which produces television and film content and operates Universal theme parks. The company maintains critical partnerships with providers like Verizon and T-Mobile to support its expanding mobile phone service segment.

In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached nearly $123 billion, which represents a slight decrease of approximately 0.2% compared to the prior year. Net income for this period was roughly $11.3 billion.

Walt Disney focuses on its entertainment, sports, and experiences segments to drive global engagement. The company leverages iconic franchises through Disney+ and Hulu while managing a massive portfolio of theme parks and cruise lines. It also holds strategic stakes in other platforms, including a 70% interest in FuboTV (FUBO -11.94%) and a 37% interest in JioStar in India.

Comcast faces heavy competition from wireline and wireless broadband providers like Charter Communications (CHTR -3.34%). The continued rise of streaming services threatens the profitability of its linear network agreements and traditional video packages. Furthermore, technological shifts such as generative artificial intelligence and a $117.5 million data breach settlement represent significant operational hurdles.

Walt Disney has an intense rivalry for viewers and advertising dollars and competes with tech giants like Amazon (AMZN -4.10%) and Apple (AAPL -1.90%). Operational risks include the potential for labor strikes among park employees or entertainment guilds, as well as service blackouts during contract negotiations. Additionally, the company must manage the volatility of consumer spending on high-end vacations and cruise ship voyages.

Comcast trades at a significant discount based on its forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, and its price-to-sales (P/S) ratio, which measures market value against sales over the past twelve months.

Deciding between Disney and Comcast really comes down to what you're looking to accomplish with your portfolio, as well as your risk tolerance. That said, between the two, I would lean toward owning Comcast over Disney.

One of the main reasons is that investors seem to be taking on less expectation risk with Comcast than with Disney. In the third quarter of 2026, Comcast generated $4.2 billion in free cash flow, giving it significant flexibility amid considerable uncertainty in the markets and the economy. While still impressive, Disney's free cash flow of $3 billion in its third quarter is noticeably less.

For Comcast, its broadband business has some issues, but its wireless segment is growing quickly and could offset weakness in that division if it continues to expand.

Disney may be a more exciting investment and has more stock price growth potential. Still, in this kind of market, I'd rather own the stock that generates more free cash flow and passes it on to its shareholders through a dividend that yields 5.3%.

#2948. The Wizards have a chance to advance in the NBA Cup

The Washington Wizards won against the Chicago Bulls last Friday. This wasn't just another regular season win. It's also their second win in NBA Cup group play, a franchise record (I'll go over why in a bit). Washington also improves to 2-1 in East Group C play.

Washington has one more game for the NBA Cup which is against the Boston Celtics on Tuesday. If they win, Washington improves to 3-1 but are mathematically eliminated from winning East Group C. It is possible that the Wizards could make the knockout stage as a wild card team if the Celtics win on Friday against the Atlanta Hawks. This would give the Celtics, Hawks and Wizards 3-1 records with the Celtics winning the group.

Now how do the Wizards claim a wildcard spot as a second place team? That's through cumulative point differential in regulation. Currently, the Wizards are third in the wildcard standings behind the Cleveland Cavaliers (+21) and the Hawks (+13) who have the same point differential as the Wizards but the Hawk hold the tiebreaker.

It will be a sign of progress if Washington can make the knockout stage of the NBA Cup. This is because Washington has finished in last place every year since 2023-24 when this tournament was introduced. In the first two years of this tournament, the Wizards finished with 0-4 group play records, while they went 1-3 last season. The Wizards also set a record two wins in group play this season, which is encouraging.

Hopefully, luck will be on their side this week when they play the Celtics on Tuesday.

(And yes, I know they host the Orlando Magic tonight).

#2941. Giants-Jaguars: Instant grades after New York’s victory over Jacksonville

The New York Giants defeated the now 7-3 Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday to advance to 6-3-1. New York controlled the game, and Jacksonville was sloppy and undisciplined for much of the game. Still, the Giants' inability to put down an opponent after establishing a lead caused some fear in the second half. New York was up 20-6 at halftime, and was receiving the ball, but a missed Dominic Zvada field goal and a fumble by Cam Skattebo set an unfortunate tone for the offense throughout the second half.

New York went three-and-out three times in the second half, and four-and-out once. The offense continues to struggle, but the defense responded well. New York went 4 of 15 on third down and finished with just 238 yards of offense, but 13 Jacksonville penalties, two turnovers, and constant pressure on Trevor Lawrence were enough for New York to earn the victory. Here are the immediate grades from the Giants' sixth win of the season

The Giants offense struggled again. They were particularly bad in the second half. J.J. McCarthy finished 18 of 38 for 173 yards with a touchdown — a bad 4.6 yards per completion. McCarthy also missed some big-time throws to Darnell Mooney. He did have 33 yards on the ground and came up with a critical 19-yard pass to Malachi Fields to seal the victory after struggling throughout the second half; he went seven straight throws with an incompletion in the second half. It wasn't pretty, but the offense did enough to get the win.

Jameis Winston handled the red zone duties on the Giants' first touchdown drive. He checked out of a run and threw a bad ball to Isaiah Likely that could have been caught. The Giants went for it on fourth down, and Winston scored on the tush push.

New York struggled to consistently run the football. They averaged just 3.1 yards per carry, and that's beefed up by McCarthy's 4.7 YPC. Cam Skattebo — who had a costly fumble in the second half — had 14 carries for just 34 yards, but did catch three passes for 14 yards. Devin Singletary received snaps to spell Skattebo, but neither running back did much on the ground. The pass protection from Skattebo, though, was good, from what I could tell, once again.

The Giants' receivers only had 173 collective yards; 55 were to Malik Nabers, who secured seven of 12 targets with a touchdown. Malachi Fields caught a key 19-yard dig route that helped the Giants secure the victory, but the offense — in general — was quiet for much of the game. We did see Jalin Hyatt catch one pass for 4 yards and Xavier Gipson had a catch for 6 yards. Darnell Mooney created a lot of separation, but could not secure any of his five targets — McCarthy missed him badly on a deep post route.

The Giants tight ends were not heavily involved. Isaiah Likely caught one pass for 35 yards, and Chris Manhertz caught one ball for 14 yards. Theo Johnson had a clutch 15-yard grab over the middle of the field on third down, but Skattebo fumbled on the next play.

The Giants offensive line struggled early against Jacksonville; J.J. McCarthy faced two free rushers on the first two plays of the game. The pass blocking stabilized, and McCarthy was only sacked once, albeit there were too many free rushers. The offensive line struggled to create space at the point of attack, which is an annoying reality that has persisted for much of the season. Overall, the offensive line was less than stellar.

D.J. Reader picked up a first-quarter sack of Trevor Lawrence after a game shared with Abdul Carter, who spun back inside to help Reader finish the sack. New York's defense was STOUT and shut down Jacksonville's rushing attack. The defensive performance was an A+ overall, with Reader highlighted for four tackles and a sack, and C.J. Okoye with one STOP on early downs. Shelby Harris contributed three tackles.

Abdul Carter told the world to WATCH and he SHOWED UP with a big-time first quarter sack and a second down sack in the second quarter, as well as some valuable pressures. He timed the snap magnificently and strung moves together all game. Carter was sensational. However, Jacksonville figured out his timing in the fourth quarter, and drew an encroachment penalty.

Kayvon Thibodeaux was flying around the field and making important assisted tackles in short-yardage situations. He had a free run — as Dennard Wilson is one to dial up — at Trevor Lawrence, but could not get him on the ground. Dawuane Smoot had a sack negated, but continues to be a solid practice squad call-up.

The Giants linebackers were flying all over the field. Arvell Reese remains a heavy hammer that punishes offensive players. Micah McFadden missed a key fourth-down tackle on the Jaguars' first offensive drive, but he made several tackles throughout the game, including a few short-yardage stops. McFadden had Lawrence tee'd up multiple times throughout the game but struggled to get him down to the deck. McFadden was dinged up at the end of the game after missing a tackle in space against Chris Rodriguez Jr. Both McFadden and Arvell Reese had seven tackles; Zaire Barnes saw snaps and had four tackles.

The Giants used multiple cornerbacks in the game, as Greg Newsome II and Tae Banks missed time during the contest. Tae Banks made an early impact by intercepting Trevor Lawrence on the Jaguars' second offensive drive. Dru Phillips had a pair of HUGE pass deflections: one on a fourth-and-one route in the red zone and the other on third-and-goal with 3:43 left in the game, which prompted Cam Little's fourth field goal. He did, though, miss a few tackles. Phillips did surrender a third-and-twenty on a deep corner versus Washington.

Paulson Adebo received snaps after Newsome left and did not return; he made a great play on the football in Cover-4 on a deep post to Parker Washington on a first-down shot that went INC. And then, on the following play, Paulson Adebo intercepted Trevor Lawrence on a possible miscommunication with a Jaguars receiver.

Jevon Holland set a tone early by dislodging the football from Parker Washington. Holland was around the line of scrimmage making tackles, and he almost came away with an interception in the end zone on Jacksonville's second drive. Holland led the team with nine tackles, and Ar'Darious Washington had three.

Dominic Zvada is frustrating. He made a kick from the right hash! It started the Giants scoring, and then the rookie booted a 54-yard field goal at the end of the first half – AGAIN – from the right hash. It's a positive development for the rookie kicker. However, Zvada then missed a 32-yard field goal from the right hash to start the third quarter, and made his fourth kick. He remains inconsistent and borderline unreliable.

Jordan Stout averaged 60 yards per punt. He is very good at what he does. Xavier Gipson handled one punt and returned it for 27 yards, while also looking capable on his kickoff returns. The kick coverage failed on the first kickoff of the game, but Tyler Nubin made his presence known multiple times on coverage plays — he finished the game with three tackles and is becoming one of the best special teams players on the team.

#2940. Knicks Bulletin: ‘I like the city of Portland’

If you are like me, you thought you could go to bed early yesterday.

If you are like me, then you realize you were not doing so, because at the end of the day it's the Knicks and they do (yes, after the championship too) Knicks things.

Oh, well, good for all, we stayed awake, and tears rained at the end of the day.

On Mikal Bridges maintaining his composure through a tough start to the season:

"He's the same. Whether he's quote-unquote struggling, he just keeps playing and he doesn't let anything impact him. He's gonna let it fly, and if he can push it, he's gonna push it. He's gonna try to defend, but he's not gonna get too high. He's not gonna get too low, and he's been there and done that. So for him to have the ball in his hands at that point in the game, there's a lot of confidence not only coming from him, but from his teammates and the staff."

On managing the rotation without Karl-Anthony Towns and OG Anunoby:

"I have an idea. I always try to go into the game with a game plan with my minutes sheet. Very seldom do I follow it. We'll have a minutes sheet going into the game."

On Landry Shamet's effort, shooting and defensive versatility:

"I felt he was a really good basketball player coming in. The biggest thing is he plays hard. So even when he's not shooting — because he hasn't shot the ball great every single game — but when he's not shooting the ball, you still feel his impact.

"He plays so hard. He's probably asked to come out of games more than anybody else because he really gasses himself being out there. Every play is that meaningful to him.

"Obviously, you can't leave him open. He's been knocking down shots for the most part. We put him on the ball in pick-and-roll situations, guarding pick-and-roll guys; we put him off the ball so he's had to chase guys. We've even put him on bigger wings and he's done a heck of a job fighting those wings. He's been phenomenal for us. We hope he continues to be that way."

On Shamet exceeding his expectations and being capable of starting for winning teams:

"It's a good question. I didn't know if he'd be this], because I think he can start for a lot of teams in this league, and I'm talking winning teams, not just any old team, but for winning teams.

"I didn't necessarily look at him that way, but I did feel he was definitely a rotational player for this team, because again, you can't teach some of the things that he does out on the floor. They're special. And it's hard to teach that, but in the same breath, you need it in order to have some success, in my opinion."

On James Wiseman's performance against Portland:

"I thought James was great. He ran the floor in both directions, he talked defensively, he impacted the ball at the rim in a phenomenal way. I thought he was really good in his minutes."

On the importance of quick decisions and purposeful movement in the Knicks' offense:

"We have to make sure that every time we cut, it's a scoring cut and our decisions are quick."

On Shamet's off-ball movement creating opportunities for teammates:

"You can tell when a guy goes from Point A to Point B with a little bit of velocity. A guy like Landry Shamet, he is doing it every single time. With him shooting the ball the way he's shooting it, that gravity that he carries when he moves, you can't really see it or feel it if you don't know the game well. But when he moves that quickly from Point A to Point B, everybody is just leaning just a little bit in that direction, which may create an opening or an advantage for your teammate that's away from him."

On getting every Knicks player to move aggressively without the ball:

"Trying to get everybody to do that all the time is huge. Because the defense doesn't have a chance to catch up, they don't have a chance to get set, and they just gotta react. And sometimes they'll overreact because you're going so hard. And you can see it as the game goes along. If guys aren't doing it, we try to mention it to him."

On Deni Avdija's ability to draw fouls and influence officials:

"For a young guy, he's one of the best in the NBA when it comes to gamesmanship with the officials. On Avdija's development as a shooter and offensive threat:

"He's figured it out at a really young age. He's also worked extremely hard on his 3-point game, so you can't give him space. You gotta play up on him, and now he's strong enough and quick enough to go through you and get by you and finish and/or get fouled. He's a handful."

On intentionally pairing Jose Alvarado with Jalen Brunson:

"A lot of times we'll pair Jose and Jalen together and we went into that consciously thinking about doing that against Minnesota, and tonight we'll go into the game consciously thinking about it so all three of those guys will play."

On discovering the Alvarado-Brunson combination against Toronto:

"Against Toronto in the second game, we threw Jose out there with Jalen and we liked it but that was not on my minutes sheet. Going into our last game … he was actually on the minutes sheet to play with Jalen some, and I kinda liked that combination."

On Tyler Kolek remaining part of the guard rotation:

"Tyler's been playing well so Tyler will play some without Jose and/or Jalen on the floor."

On rarely following any predetermined rotation plan:

On allowing players' families to travel with the team to build trust:

"In order to get players' trust and get true connectivity, it's anybody associated with them. That's why it's important to have families around."

On Mikal Bridges overcoming his shooting struggles through consistent work:

"Yeah, that's just who he is. I don't know how many times I've said this before, but when you continue to put work in your game every single day, and things may not be falling in your favor, but you keep doing the right thing every single day, you keep chipping away, chipping away. Eventually, things are gonna turn for you. And over the past week or two, things have been turning for him, and now he's on a roll."

On repeatedly hitting game-winning shots against Portland:

"I like the city of Portland. [Damian Lillard] is one of my best friends. I like the city of Portland."

On maintaining his effort and making plays in crunch time:

"I try to play hard throughout the whole game, and obviously when the time gets short and it's time to win a game, I think everybody's senses are heightened. Just try to win a game and make a play."

"Yeah, just trying to get Jalen open and create space. How Josh threw it kind of indicated I was going to be open, so just go make a play. It's great. First, you win the game, but second, seeing the joy in those guys. Obviously, tonight with the alumni stuff, it's a pretty cool moment to be in that situation, especially after a tough fourth quarter. So it felt good."

On sharing Bridges' struggles while adjusting to the season:

"Me and him are in the same boat… we're trying to figure it out."

On Bridges remaining prepared despite his early-season struggles:

"Knowing that any good and bad stretch in the NBA can change very quickly, he's always in a position to put himself in a good situation."

On Bridges' game-winner rescuing the Knicks after their fourth-quarter collapse and his dumb late foul:

"Shoutout to Mikal for making the big-time 3, to kind of mask the nonsense that happened."

On the Karl-Anthony Towns unfair criticism during his years in Minnesota:

"When we first got him in Minnesota, the playoffs, they were saying how he's a very good player that couldn't win, couldn't get the team to the playoffs. Then, when we got to the playoffs, any time we struggled, it was him that took the fall, unfairly. And I think it was great to see not only the impact that he had on this championship team, but to see the way that he's playing now. … I love KAT; I was happy for him to get to the mountaintop; I was happy for him to play a major role.

"Then, when we made a deep run, they said you can't win a title with him, and he got the blame."

#2938. Chegg: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Chegg's push into student employability and corporate skilling is the piece to watch, since it decides whether revenue can rebuild once the legacy homework business fades.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:12PM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 3, 2026, Chegg (CHGG -5.30%) announced that it has fully repaid its debt and completed a balance sheet reset. The company is shedding its declining legacy homework help business to focus on student employability and career skilling. That pivot determines whether the business can rebuild sustainable revenue. Three things management said on the call stand out.

Management trimmed expenses to keep the business profitable on an adjusted EBITDA basis, which measures core operating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. Paying off all remaining debt leaves the company with cash holdings to reinvest into new product lines.

Chegg launched a job platform on internships.com to capture students seeking career placement, partnering directly with universities through business-to-institution pilots. Helping colleges demonstrate career outcomes for graduates creates a direct institutional channel for student growth.

Expanding corporate skilling allows the business to deliver enterprise training packages through third-party platforms in business-to-business arrangements. Broadening these partner channels helps diversify revenue beyond individual consumer subscriptions.

Legacy academic declines are stabilizing while new skilling and employability launches pick up traction. Chegg relies on operational efficiency, reduced capital expenditures (CapEx), and artificial intelligence (AI) tools to protect cash flow as it tracks user engagement.

Management continues to evaluate targeted acquisitions alongside organic platform enhancements to accelerate growth.

#2933. These 5 Stocks Could Double by 2028. Here's What Has to Go Right.

SpaceX, Broadcom, SentinelOne, SoundHound, and Dutch Bros have the potential to double.

By Geoffrey Seiler – Nov 23, 2026 at 12:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Space Exploration Technologies ›

When you're investing in individual stocks, you're always looking for a few that have the potential to double in a couple of years. Not every investment will pan out, but a few big winners will help lead to strong overall performance. Let's look at five growth stocks that have the potential to double by 2028 and what would need to happen for them to achieve that.

Despite its size, SpaceX (SPCX -7.69%) has clear potential to double in the next two years. For this to happen, it's going to have to grow rapidly and continue to hit important technological milestones, like it did when it recently caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket.

Much of SpaceX's growth in the next two years will come from its infrastructure-as-a-service business. To quickly grow this business, it's going to add a lot of compute capacity while maintaining its strong payback periods. If it can navigate permitting issues and industry bottlenecks and hit its growth targets of adding 10 gigawatts of power next year, and do that again in 2028, the stock could double.

The market is shifting toward custom artificial intelligence (AI) chips and inference, which plays right into Broadcom's (AVGO -12.19%) wheelhouse. With the stock trading at a forward price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of just 11 times fiscal 2028 analyst estimates (ending October 2028), it has a big opportunity to double in the next two years.

For this to happen, the company is going to have to maintain solid hardware gross margins and not lose significant share in the application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) market to cheaper competitors in future chip iterations. It's also going to have to see large customers Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) and OpenAI thrive, as much of its future projected custom chip revenue is coming from these two customers and Alphabet (GOOGL -2.70%) (GOOG -2.59%).

Trading at a huge discount to larger cybersecurity rivals while growing quickly, SentinelOne (S -4.58%) stock could easily double from continued growth and multiple expansion. Right now, the stock trades at a forward price-to-sales (P/S) multiple of 6 times 2027 estimates compared to 17.5 times for Palo Alto Networks (PANW -5.09%) and 37 times for CrowdStrike (CRWD -5.76%), so the opportunity for significant multiple expansion is there.

The company has been aggressively making moves to become a strong provider in the AI era, and if this leads to accelerating growth, the stock has a great opportunity to double. Analysts at Wedbush, meanwhile, noted after talking to vendors and resellers that customers were starting to expand with SentinelOne solutions, and the company was winning in the small and medium-sized business (SMB) and mid-market spaces due to its strong abilities and cheaper pricing.

Beaten to a pulp over the past two years, SoundHound AI (SOUN -10.31%) has the potential to see its stock double in the coming years, with its valuation down to a forward P/S multiple under 6. For this to happen, it will need to stabilize and integrate its recent LivePerson acquisition, hit its target of becoming earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) profitable in the second half of 2027, and see strong adoption of OASYS, its new voice, language intelligence, and agentic AI orchestration solution.

The ingredients are all there; it will just be a matter of execution. Right now, the market is betting SoundHound won't be able to pull this off, but if it does, the upside is enormous.

Stepping outside of the tech sector, Dutch Bros (BROS -4.01%) has one of the best opportunities in the consumer space for its stock to double over the next two years. The coffee shop operator has been delivering strong same-store sales growth while it has huge expansion opportunities. However, the stock has been beaten down over the past year, leaving it at a very attractive P/S valuation compared to rival Starbucks (SBUX -1.28%) despite its much longer growth runway.

If Dutch Bros can consistently deliver better-than-expected, same-store sales growth over the next two years while growing its store base, its stock should be able to double. Some of its initiatives to drive same-store growth include menu expansion, including food; order ahead; its loyalty program; and piloting third-party delivery.

#2931. Inside the Suns: Ryan Dunn, Koa Peat, a wake up call?

Welcome to Inside the Suns, a deep down analysis of the current Phoenix Suns team in which the Fantable — a round table of Bright Siders — give their takes on the Suns' latest issues and news.

GuarGuar: I've been really impressed with Ryan so far this season. He's showing more control and poise in his game. He's not recklessly driving at 100 mph to the rim every time he touches the ball. The jump shot mechanics look better, and he's been impressive as a roll man this year. He's been a pleasant surprise.

zenzino: I love it! How could I not? As I wrote in a previous Fantable (or thread, I can't remember), Dunn was considered by many (including me) to be the odd man out for rotational minutes this season. However, he became the poster child for the fact that progress is not linear. After a sophomore year where the improvement was slight (especially alongside Oso's improvement), Dunn has made a leap in his third year.

We never questioned his defense. He reportedly put in a lot of work on his shot this off-season. As he said himself, he 'has to trust in the work'. This becomes evident during a game. When he has time to think about it, he'll either pass up a shot or look more like last year's shooting. When he doesn't have time to think, his shot looks really good and goes in more often than not.

The more he works, and the less time he has to think, the shots will go down, and he'll gain enough confidence to think and shoot.

This is also a lesson not to give up on Sheer. He may have a sophomore slump this season, but that doesn't mean he's not working and could come out later in the season or his third year to make a Dunn-like leap.

Ashton: I am a little curious why Dunn's minutes seem to vary by game. He is clearly the next man up at the power forward position. But, thus far, I have not paid enough attention to Dunn on the Fantable and he is impressing me as a future breakout candidate to start. So, my bad on not giving Ryan Dunn more love early.

Also, Brooks said he would be willing to play bench minutes? Jaw hits the floor as he is coming off one of his best games against the Sacramento Kings. He stated that is to work on his playmaking with the better spacing that the bench provides. I applaud his heroic statement, but I am calling BS. The real reason is so he can terrorize opposing bench unit defenses into therapy with his constant chirping. Still, an intriguing thought to consider. Does Ott buy-in? I doubt it.

That would make Ryan Dunn the starter for minutes if that were to come true. Some of the Suns' lineups would be rife for consideration in the comment sections.

OldAz: Personally, I love what Ryan has done this year. He has taken advantage of the lowered expectations, especially compared to last season when he was expected to come in and capture a larger role only to struggle with the new system and get stuck behind a number of veteran guards.

This season, most had written him off coming into the season and were fine throwing him into whatever trade would accomplish moving whatever core player that fan wanted to move. Instead, he ratcheted up his defensive intensity and the speed at which he plays and has made a significant impact.  My only complaint is with the coaching staff that seems to have way too long of a leash for veteran players to play emotionless, effortless basketball and only give a player like Ryan a few minutes despite their obvious positive impact on the overall result on the floor.

Ryan is not going to fill up the stat sheet, but he is going to hustle on defense, compete for rebounds, and is willing to shoot or drive when he is left open.  He is a perfect complement to Booker or any of the other "star" players on the court when Ott chooses to play him.  He is one of those players (along with Goodwin, Gillespie, and Kennard) that you can pair with either center and 2 of the core starters and get a pretty decent lineup because of their hustle and energy. The only difference is he is the only one of those 4 that also brings some length to the court.

I'm not overly worried about the recent little injuries, as I believe he has figured out that his energy and effort mean more than the stats he puts up each night. Hopefully Ott is starting to figure out the same thing.

Rod: I hated to see him get hurt in the Jazz game. Hopefully. he won't be out long because he's become an important part of the Suns' rotation. His offensive impact hasn't been great, but he's been playing more under control on that end and making positive contributions, both inside (5th most dunks on the team in just the 10th most minutes per game) and outside (42.3% from three). His biggest areas of impact have been on defense and in rebounding (per 36, he's tied with Bridges for 2nd at 8.6).

I'll admit that I was one of the people who was almost ready to give up on Ryan this season if he didn't show some improvement. Happily, he's come through for us and is playing very well and under control.

GuarGuar: I really hope it was a wake-up call. This starting lineup has been awful together, and the metrics don't lie. The Jalen Green PG experiment has been an abject failure, and the sooner we move off of it, the better we will be. The bench plays together as a unit and with a ton of energy, the complete opposite of our starting unit.

zenzino: I guess? How many wake-up calls do they need?

They supposedly had one in the first game of the season. The first game!

They definitely looked better against Denver and really came out against the Kings with aggressiveness, energy, and surprisingly good ball movement. It was the Kings, but maybe playing a few easier games in a row (Jazz & Pels next) will allow them to get some confidence/momentum.

Recent reports amidst all the trade rumors/ideas say that the Suns are not shopping Green. They like the roster they have and are content to give these guys time to gel. I don't know if it has anything to do with the benching, but we're definitely seeing some improvement.

It occurred to me the other day that it is the fans' job to (over)react from game to game and the coaches/FO's job NOT to react from game to game.

Ashton: I hate this question. Beat LA, Beat LA!

The fact of the matter is that the Lakers are that good. It was a nice salve to the wounds to see the Suns beat a good Nuggets team the day after. Which is exactly what the Suns need: beating the teams they are supposed to beat, but picking up a few wins against the teams that are not (Houston and Denver). The Lakers were not on the bingo card in the W category.

Still, Ott probably wisely threw in the towel against a very good Lakers squad and allowed his starters to watch real basketball from the sidelines without getting injured. I was fine with it from a strategic point of view, but I am not fine with it from a fan point of view.

OldAz: Maybe. It certainly couldn't have hurt as we have seen a better version of Brooks and Green since then, with more focus on the defensive end and moving the ball on offense instead of always forcing their own shots. I think Booker and Bridges were already playing well, but it really requires all the starters to be on the same page for that group to succeed.  The better play and effort from all has also allowed Ott to play a little more randomly with lineups.

Now the question is if the recent successes are more about this improved play and more diverse lineup combinations, or just a product of playing lesser teams that the Suns should handle like the Kings and Jazz.

Rod: You could call it that, or you could call it a message from Ott, "Play with some heart or you'll sit and watch your teammates show you what that means." Whatever you want to call it, it seems to have worked in the games since then.

You can have all the talent in the world, but without effort, players are just wasting the fans' time (and patience) when they're just going through the motions. I don't want to see the starters playing like that again, and hopefully they got that message from Ott loud and clear…and won't forget it.

GuarGuar: Koa is probably only useful as a small-ball 5 right now until he develops a jump shot, which looks to be a ways away. He has good instincts and can finish through contact pretty well, but he's not close to being ready for a consistent rotation spot in my opinion. Next year will probably be a different discussion.

zenzino: I think it's pretty telling that he has spent zero time with the Valley Suns. My wild speculation is that Ott wants him with the team and ready to play.

After looking great in quality minutes against the Lakers, Ott teased us with a 2nd-quarter appearance of Peat against the Nuggets. That lasted a minute. Literally. The next time we saw him was garbage time against the hapless Kings.

When this question was first sent to us at the beginning of the week, my answer was that Koa should definitely get some Brooks minutes. Or even some Bridges minutes. But mostly Brooks.

Up through the Lakers game, Brooks has been a shell of what we loved about him last season. Maybe, like cutting Sampson's hair (and Dillon's hair), Dillon's effort to not get techs this season has stripped him of his strength.

He was better against the Nuggets (got a tech) and was on fire against the Kings (no tech). Hopefully, he has turned a corner and will continue with the aggressive Villain we know and love. Techs and all.

Bridges is showing progress with every game, and we are beginning to see what the FO envisioned with this addition. 14 games is not even close to enough games for a starter to fully integrate. As I said, the FO has to take the long view and not overreact game to game.

So, barring injuries or a slide by either Brooks or Bridges, we will probably only see Koa in very specific matchup situations or garbage time. That's ok for now. There's a lot to learn from just being with the team. Especially if they continue the winning trend.

Ashton: How to answer this one? Peat's best game came against the Lakers. At least the Arizona guy gets it. But in the end, stats do not lie on small sample sizes. I am stealing a copy and paste from Hoops Nightly:

Peat has appeared in 8 games and averages 4.5 minutes, 3.1 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.1 assists. He is shooting 64.7 percent from the field and 100.0 percent at the line, with a 0.0 mark from three. His true shooting is 68.2 percent and his usage is 21.1. The plus-minus is 3.8. These numbers come from very few minutes, so they say little yet. His minutes have ranged from 1.3 to 8.2 in a night, and he has not scored in three of the eight games.

Okay, with that out of the way (I hate talking stats – leave that to the board members), the stats still suggest that Peat's minutes should increase if only to increase the sample size. And consistent minutes would probably help rather than 8 minutes here and a throw-in one minute there.

Since the question asked if he "looks" ready for more rotational minutes, I would state an emphatic yes until proven otherwise.

OldAz: In small doses, certainly.  Just like we saw in the Jazz game, he needs to learn to play at this level without fouling, but that isn't going to happen at the G League level or during garbage minutes when the refs also just want to get the game over.

I think he should get about the same 5-6 minutes Dunn was getting earlier in the season, and given an opportunity to play more as he does well. To me, these minutes should be coming from Brooks, Green, Bridges, and even Booker, as up until the last few games the bench minutes have been better anyway, so Ott might as well mix and match more minutes with just 2 of those core 4 on the floor with a center and 2 bench players. Go ahead and compress the starters' minutes while this is working, save more strain on the starters' legs until later in the season and see who actually develops.

I know this will never happen, but the Suns really have to come up with a better way to give minutes to young players at the NBA level and start developing them faster than they have been.

Rod: Peat does look ready for more playing time, but for now, I think most of that time will come when Ott decides to play a small-ball lineup, so I don't think he'll be taking minutes away from anyone specifically. I've seen Ott try various players out in that role, and Koa just seems to be the best fit in that role. And considering the guy's built like a linebacker, I'm not at all certain that we should even call it "small" ball when he's at the 5.

The three quick fouls he got in the Jazz game don't change my mind. He may not be ready for a full-blown rotation spot, but he's ready for spot rotation minutes.

As always, many thanks to our Fantable members for all their extra effort this week!

"You can see his (Jalen Green's) speed. Anytime he's in open court, anytime he gets downhill, that's what we need. We need paint pressure. We're a predominantly jump-shooting team. Him and Miles (Bridges) provide some of that paint pressure, that downhill thrust that we need offensively." – Jordan Ott

"We're just gonna continue to talk about just stacking our small segments of time and that will build continually over time. We'll get better. We believe in that. We believe every time we're together, whether that's a meal, whether that's a shootaround, whether that's a film session, that we have to go all in, all in, all the time, and they'll continually stack." – Jordan Ott

"Collectively, we were in it for the full 48." – Jordan Ott

"I see Man-Man working every day. He's one of the hardest workers I've ever played with." – Miles Bridges

"We have guys that want to win, that want to play the right way." – Luke Kennard

On November 23, 1972, Charlie Scott recorded the Phoenix Suns' first-ever triple-double with 42 points, 10 rebounds, and 15 assists in a 128-122 victory over the Detroit Pistons on Thanksgiving Day.

On November 23, 1994, Wesley Person hit for 19 points to lead 10 double-figure scorers in Phoenix's 140-109 home win over the LA Clippers. The Suns became the third team in NBA history to have 10 different players score in double figures in the same game. No Suns player shot less than 50% from the field that day, and the team FG percentage was 64.7% while also hitting 47.1% of their three-point attempts.

On November 23, 2015, Devin Booker got his first career start for the Phoenix Suns, filling in for an injured Eric Bledsoe. Booker had 4 points, 1 assist, 4 rebounds, and 1 steal in his debut in the Suns' starting lineup as Phoenix fell to the San Antonio Spurs 98-84.

On November 24, 1989, the Suns reserves were outscored 16-0 to start the 4th quarter, so "only" up 28 points, head coach Cotton Fitzsimmons brought back his starters, allowing Jeff Hornacek to record the first triple-double of his career (22pts, 12 rebs, 15assists) in a 121-94 win over the Orlando Magic.

On November 25, 1995, down 110-100 with 90 seconds left, the Suns nailed 4 three-pointers and, after Nick Van Exel inexplicably allowed himself to be tied up with 6.7 seconds left, Michael Finley hit a buzzer-beater to defeat the LA Lakers, 114-113.

On November 27, 1977, Paul Westphal set a new franchise and career-high when he scored 48 points in a 115-97 win over the Denver Nuggets. Westphal was on fire all night, shooting 20-30 from the field and 8-10 FTs. When John MacLeod pulled him with 3:17 left in the game, fans began to chant, "We want Westy."

#2929. Innodata's 2027 Outlook: AI Data Engineering Pivot Drives High-Value Lifecycle Contracts

This under-the-radar AI services stock boasts a Superscore of 82 from our Hidden Gems Primary database, part of The Motley Fool's Moneyball Database system. Here's why.

By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 23, 2026 at 12:26AM EST

In the quiet town of Ridgefield Park, New Jersey, sits a company that has spent 35 years building the infrastructure for other people's technology. For most of its history, Innodata (INOD -8.91%) was a back-office service provider, the kind of company that handled mundane data tasks that big tech companies couldn't be bothered with.

Then came the generative artificial intelligence boom, and the company found itself sitting on a pile of human-annotated data that frontier model labs desperately needed. The stock, trading at $28.12 as of the week ending Nov. 20, 2026, has seen its price decline more than 40% over the past year, reflecting the market's ongoing reassessment of the company's growth trajectory and project-based revenue volatility.

Our proprietary Hidden Gems scoring system assigns Innodata an overall Superscore of 82 out of 100, placing it in the Strong category. The Superscore is an AI-powered score that evaluates a company's overall strength by combining financial performance, product market position, technological capabilities, leadership quality, and relative valuation. It represents the unification of all our scores into a single score for public companies, with five rating bands: Exceptional (90-100), Strong (75-89), Above Average (60-74), Average (40-59), and Cautious (0-39).

An 82 places Innodata in the Top ~7% of every company we score, ahead of roughly 93 out of every 100 companies we evaluate. This score is a single data-driven signal, and this research pairs the strengths with the risks so you can weigh both sides before doing more work.

Innodata maintains a high return on net tangible assets, which means the business earns outsized profits on a small base of hard physical equipment. This efficiency allows the company to turn each point of revenue growth into meaningful returns, which helps explain why investors might pay a premium for the shares despite the underlying execution risks.

The Hidden Gems Superscore reflects The Motley Fool's proprietary AI-driven evaluation of a company across product, financial, leadership, and valuation pillars as of the article date and may change over time. Performance figures are point-in-time. Past performance does not guarantee future results.

You may want to keep researching before buying if...

The Superscore is just one signal in your research process; always weigh these findings against your personal financial goals and risk tolerance before making any investment decision.

Thanks to the massive AI tailwind, Innodata is poised to see sales growth in the coming years. That's because the organizations building AI models need the software to deliver results that are accurate, safe, and reliable. Innodata is a key enabler of that outcome.

Consequently, the enterprise is now building a business pipeline with the U.S. government, including work with the Department of War and Navy. Its quality of work is of such high caliber that when AI researchers switch companies, they call Innodata to help them at the new organization.

Revenue concentration among a subset of customers is a concern, but Innodata is working to diversify. As an example of its progress here, even though it lost a project with one of its traditionally largest customers, the company still raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance to 42% or more year over year, up from 40%, as new projects come online.

Innodata is also benefiting from the rise of physical AI, where it is using motion capture of human movement to train humanoid robots how to move like people. Through these numerous AI-fueled opportunities, Innodata is well positioned to see its business grow in the years ahead.

#2927. Joe Mazzulla downplays disastrous third straight loss: ‘We played well enough’

For the third straight time, the Boston Celtics went out like a dud, collapsing against the two-win Sacramento Kings on Saturday night without Jayson Tatum, Derrick White and Mitchell Robinson. But head coach Joe Mazzulla was rather dismissive afterward.

"I think we played well enough to win the game," Mazzulla told reporters, per CLNS Media, after Boston's 97-96, "and they made more shots than we did, and made a couple of more plays down the stretch. You take a look at the process of the game, we played well and lost. So that's what you take from [it] and move on to tomorrow."

Mazzulla turned to Paul George and Payton Pritchard to lead the pack. They shared the floor with Sam Hauser, Hugo González and Neemias Queta in Boston's starting lineup. Yet the team's strongest and most efficient contribution didn't come from any of them. It came from 39-year-old guard Mike Conley, who had made just four appearances for Boston entering the night, averaging eight minutes per game before receiving 18 minutes off the bench in Sacramento.

Conley scored 19 points, converting his first six consecutive shot attempts, while adding four rebounds, three assists and two steals. From the looks of it, Conley had himself a heroic, game-saving performance in the works, good enough to get the Celtics back in the column. He was active, up to speed and turned back the clock to his vintage Memphis Grizzlies days, even though he sat on the bench for the entire first and third quarters.

Nov 21, 2026; Sacramento, California, USA; Boston Celtics forward Paul George (13) reacts during the third quarter against the Sacramento Kings at Golden 1 Center. Mandatory Credit: Justine Willard-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Had it not been for Conley's out-of-the-blue scoring outburst, the Kings might've run the Celtics out of the building.

"He kept us in it," Mazzulla said. "Tried to finish the game with him as much as we could. Thought he was great on both ends of the floor and tonight's the reason why you have a guy like that on your roster, and he gave us a chance to win tonight."

Conley stood tall as Boston's lone bright spot, tying George for the team's lead in scoring while finishing as Boston's plus-minus leader (+17).

The Celtics performed well below their standard, underscoring the impact Tatum's absence had against a Kings team that leads the Western Conference in turnovers (17.5), boasts the NBA's second-lowest-scoring offense (106.8 points) and had won just one of its first 15 games entering Saturday night.

Without their superstar, the wheels fell off the wagon.

In the third quarter, Mazzulla's group got outscored 35-13 and went 0-for-13 from three.

With back-to-back rest days, the underperformance was all the more inexcusable.

Boston finished the night shooting 33.7 percent from the field, going 34-for-101. They shot 22.4 percent from 3-point range, going 13-for-58 and setting a franchise record for most misses (45) in a single game. At the free-throw line, they went 15-for-25, adding further fuel to the fire.

George went 6-for-21, Pritchard went 4-for-17 and Baylor Scheierman shot 2-for-11.

Coming off consecutive losses to the Orlando Magic and Denver Nuggets, this was their ugliest dud by far.

In the fourth quarter, the Celtics traded baskets with Sacramento as the clock ticked down. Queta hit a go-ahead 3-pointer from the corner with 3:47 remaining, only for Kings rookie Darius Acuff Jr. to drain the equalizer, also from beyond the arc. George grabbed an offensive rebound and finished the putback layup with 49 seconds left. Acuff answered by drawing a foul and sinking both free throws at the other end. Pritchard sank a clutch fadeaway jumper to give Boston a 96-95 lead with 12 seconds remaining. Then the Celtics failed to protect the glass on the ensuing possession.

Acuff challenged González off the inbound, drove past him and missed his right-handed layup. But Sacramento's Keegan Murray leaped over Devin Carter to secure the offensive rebound and finish the putback, giving the Kings a 97-96 lead and leaving Boston with just five seconds for redemption.

For the game, Pritchard was handed the ball against Murray but failed to create enough space for a clean look, capping an already miserable performance with a wasted opportunity.

Pritchard finished with nine points and missed all eight of his 3-point attempts, which he owned up to.

"It's frustrating," Pritchard told reporters. "I just got to play better. I gotta do more, so a lot of that is on me in the third quarter and stuff like that. So it's my fault for that one."

Pritchard on the final possession: "Obviously didn't get to a good enough spot, and [Murray] played good defense. But probably need to try to find a better look, though."

The Celtics have lost three consecutive regular-season games for the first time since opening last season with three straight defeats. They suffered their most humbling loss yet, deservedly getting served their lunch by arguably the worst team in the NBA.

"I thought we competed at a high level through just a drought offensively where we couldn't make shots," Mazzulla said. "And again, you have to stick to the process of it. I thought we played well enough to win, and we just didn't. They made a few more plays than we did."

Winning and playing "well enough" to win aren't mutually exclusive. However, the Celtics didn't meet the threshold necessary to leave Sacramento victorious. Their result was entirely warranted.

#2926. Innodata: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Its balance sheet holds $153.7 million in cash net of prepayments and no debt, giving management room to fund research without new financing.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 23, 2026 at 12:52AM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 5, 2026, Innodata (INOD -8.91%) announced revenue of $95.6 million, up 53% year over year. The data provider is shifting from one-off model labeling into recurring training infrastructure for complex artificial intelligence systems. That shift broadens its revenue base across frontier technology labs and enterprise customers. Three takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

Innodata previously suffered from revenue concentration, relying heavily on a single main customer. Management is now expanding relationships with other technology giants, forecasting over $20 million in 2027 revenue from a major hyperscaler that generated just $3.1 million over the trailing 12 months.

Training robotics foundation models requires custom video and movement data set generation, since web-based data sets don't exist for physical actions. Building these specialized physical data sets allows the company to become critical recurring infrastructure as industrial and consumer robotics move toward commercial deployment.

The sudden termination of a major program by the company's historically largest customer creates a temporary headwind in the fourth quarter. Management expects to fill that $12 million revenue gap with replacement programs by the first quarter of 2027, illustrating how individual program lifecycles introduce short-term lumpiness.

Growth momentum builds as artificial intelligence spending shifts toward complex autonomous agents and physical robotics. The company holds structural advantages in proprietary data collection, custom simulation environments, and deep relationships with frontier research labs. Management is watching organic capital deployment and execution timelines across its expansion drivers.

With $153.7 million in cash net of customer prepayments and zero debt, the balance sheet gives the company full flexibility to fund internal research and development. Pipeline expansion across enterprise and government partners positions the business for continued top-line acceleration.

#2923. Nvidia Just Reported Its First Quarter Without Jensen Huang. If the AI Trade Is Cracking, Warren Buffett’s Advice Comes Down to 1 Move.

Buffett has age-old advice that can help you survive different market paradigms.

By Brett Schafer – Nov 23, 2026 at 1:00AM EST

It has been a rough few weeks for Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) shareholders. The stock has quickly fallen 47.5% from all-time highs due to founder Jensen Huang's ouster over an affair scandal, the potential sale of computer chips that deliberately circumvented government sanctions, and looming competition in artificial intelligence (AI) compute that could erode Nvidia's once-flaunted moat.

Some investors argue that the AI trade is cracking, and that Nvidia's future will be worse than its near past. Before buying the dip in Nvidia shares, investors should heed the long-standing advice of investing legend Warren Buffett given this latest earnings result and market volatility.

Nvidia's third-quarter numbers were fantastic. Revenue grew over 100% year over year to $116 billion, driven by growth in data center computer chips to $107.6 billion in revenue. Margins were good, with trailing operating margin hitting 66%, making Nvidia one of the most profitable companies in the world. According to the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E), Nvidia trades at just 13.5x its trailing numbers. For a business growing revenue 100% year over year, this figure looks quite cheap.

That is not what investors care about. They care about future earnings, and the predictability of future earnings just got muddied in an extreme way. First, Huang is not running the business anymore. He was wheeling and dealing to secure contracts for Nvidia computer chips in recent years. Second, the United States government is investigating Nvidia for potentially selling illegal chips to third parties that then sent them to China, and there's also a Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) investigation into its accounting statements.

Plus, its customers are either teetering on the brink financially or looking to replace Nvidia chips in their data centers. The so-called neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius Group have plunged amid funding concerns. These make up $47.5 billion of the $107.6 billion in data center revenue. Other revenue comes from hyperscalers that are all selling or researching how to build their own computer chips to lower costs for cloud customers.

There is a lot to balance when analyzing an investment in Nvidia today. Given the trading volume in the stock, many investors have looked to buy the dip, with shares down by almost half from the highs.

Buffett's advice is to avoid such complicated situations as an investor. In fact, the saying goes that Buffett wants businesses so good that even a bad CEO could run them, because if you are going to hold a stock for multiple decades, a bad leader will show up sooner or later. Therefore, you want to invest in high-quality businesses with good defensibility that are simple to understand. Nvidia is the opposite of this.

No stock better exemplifies this strategy for Buffett than Coca-Cola. The soda brand has been a long-running holding for Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway simply because it is the leader in a profitable category. No matter what happens technologically in the coming decades, people will likely still drink Coca-Cola. The same can't be said for Nvidia chips, which is why Buffett has never made it or rapidly changing technologies a part of his portfolio.

Lastly, investors should learn from Buffett's strategy more broadly to maintain wealth over the decades. He never liked participating in thematic bull markets, whether it was the dot-com bubble, housing in the early 2000s, or artificial intelligence today. Wall Street may love hot stocks for a time, and Buffett was willing to initially look dumb for avoiding them, but there is almost always a wash-out on the other side. Choosing not to get swept up in fear of missing out (FOMO) is one of the keys to Buffett's long-term success, and that will likely be the case with Berkshire Hathaway during this AI bear market as well.

The secret to Buffett's durability was not necessarily what he bought, but what he avoided as an investor over 75 years in the market.

#2919. Xerox: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Management is redesigning hardware to slash service costs, a structural shift that could reshape profitability if execution sticks.

By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 23, 2026 at 1:16AM EST

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, Xerox (XRX -0.65%) announced that it is lowering full-year profit expectations and suspending dividends to conserve cash. External cost inflation in memory and oil is squeezing margins faster than management can cut internal expenses.

Yet hardware sales ticked up for the first time in over three years, showing underlying momentum in workplace printing. Three key statements from management clarify where the business is heading.

Management lowered its full-year adjusted operating income guidance to between $450 million and $475 million. The board also halted cash payouts to shareholders, saving about $28 million annually to support debt reduction and protect total liquidity, which stood at $726 million.

Component costs expanded rapidly during the quarter, with memory rising from 2% of machine costs early in the year to 10%. Higher freight and materials prices added to those pressures, forcing management to plan portfolio price increases starting in early 2027.

Service maintenance generates over $3 billion in annual revenue, but sending technicians to fix broken machines cuts into profits. Management is designing printers with fewer internal parts and embedded artificial intelligence sensors so technical issues get resolved remotely.

Xerox faces higher input expenses, but cost reduction and debt reduction continue as planned. Integration savings from the Lexmark acquisition should yield $100 million in 2027. Management is expanding global capability centers, which are offshore internal service hubs employing 15% of staff, to increase operational efficiency.

The company is shifting balance sheet debt and enforcing stricter pricing to protect margins against entry-level hardware shifts.
